qs.q: A patient presents with chest pain after inhaling cocaine. Why are beta-blockers strictly avoided in the management of cocaine-induced chest pain?
o: Risk of enhancing central nervous system depression
Risk of causing immediate severe tachycardia
qs.e: Beta-blockers must be avoided in cocaine toxicity due to the risk of unopposed alpha-adrenoceptor stimulation, which can worsen coronary vasoconstriction. Benzodiazepines and IV nitrates are preferred instead.

qs.q: A 25-year-old man dies suddenly at a nightclub. Toxicology shows high cocaine levels. No gross cardiac pathology. Most likely histopathologic finding?
qs.e: Cocaine causes catecholamine surge via reuptake blockade, producing intense vasospasm and ischemia, resulting in contraction band necrosis — the earliest visible histopathologic change.

qs.q: Cocaine blocks the reuptake of neurotransmitters by inhibiting which transporters?
o: NET, DAT, and SERT (all three monoamine transporters)
qs.e: Cocaine is a non-selective inhibitor that blocks all three monoamine reuptake transporters: NET (norepinephrine), DAT (dopamine), and SERT (serotonin). This results in increased synaptic concentrations of all three neurotransmitters, contributing to its stimulant and addictive properties.

qs.q: Which statement about cocaine's cardiovascular toxicity is correct?
o: It can cause both tachycardia and hypertension due to increased sympathetic outflow
Cardiovascular effects only occur with chronic use
It produces bradycardia through vagal stimulation
qs.e: Cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake, leading to increased norepinephrine at sympathetic nerve terminals. This causes simultaneous tachycardia and hypertension. Additionally, at higher doses, cocaine's sodium channel blocking effects can contribute to arrhythmias and cardiac toxicity.

qs.q: The combination of cocaine and ethanol in the body produces
o: Enhanced cocaine metabolism and shorter effects
Cocaethylene, with longer half-life and similar toxicity
qs.e: When cocaine and ethanol are consumed together, they undergo transesterification in the liver to form cocaethylene, which has a half-life of 3-4 hours (longer than cocaine's ~50 min) and shares similar pharmacology. This prolongs the "high" and may increase cardiotoxicity.

qs.q: Which of the following describes the mechanism of Cocaine?
qs.e: Cocaine blocks the reuptake of catecholamines, leading to increased sympathetic activity.

ai.title: Cocaine Intoxication and Toxicity
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic that can cause acute cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric emergencies. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on history, clinical signs and basic bedside tests.

sections.p: Acute cocaine intoxication is the clinical syndrome after recent use of cocaine, characterised by heightened sympathetic activity and possible organ injury.
b: Diagnosis is clinical; confirm with urine toxicology when available.
Look for recent sniffing, smoking, injection or oral use.

sections.p: Severity is graded by organ involvement and hemodynamic stability.
b: Mild: tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, mild chest pain.
Moderate: persistent hypertension >180/110 mmHg, arrhythmia, severe chest pain, agitation.
Severe/ life‑threatening: myocardial infarction, stroke, seizures, hyperthermia >40 °C, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac arrest.

sections.p: Cocaine itself is the primary cause; co‑ingestion of other stimulants or alcohol can worsen toxicity.
b: Pure cocaine (powder or crack).
Cocaine mixed with levamisole (common adulterant).
Concurrent alcohol use → cocaethylene formation.
Co‑use of amphetamines, khat, or nicotine.

sections.p: Patients may present with a combination of cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric features.
b: Chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations.
Hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmias.
Agitation, paranoia, tactile hallucinations.
Seizures, hyperthermia, diaphoresis.
Abdominal pain from mesenteric vasospasm.

t.b: Are the vitals stable? – Guides need for urgent antihypertensive or anti‑arrhythmic therapy.
Detects ischemia, QT prolongation, arrhythmias – treat coronary spasm or arrhythmia accordingly.
Identifies myocardial injury – if unavailable, rely on clinical chest pain and ECG changes.
Confirms recent cocaine exposure – if unavailable, base decision on history and signs.
Screens for rhabdomyolysis – CK >5 000 U/L suggests muscle breakdown, need aggressive IV fluids.
Detects hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis – correct abnormalities promptly.

sections.p: Complications can be rapidly fatal and require immediate action.
b: Acute myocardial infarction or unstable angina.
Life‑threatening arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation).
Ischemic stroke or intracerebral haemorrhage.
Seizure lasting >5 min or status epilepticus.
Hyperthermia >40 °C with organ failure.
Severe rhabdomyolysis with renal impairment.

sections.p: Treat the acute toxicity first, then address complications and arrange follow‑up for substance use disorder.
b: Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give high‑flow oxygen.
Control hypertension with short‑acting IV agents (e.g., nitroglycerin, nicardipine) – avoid β‑blockers alone because of unopposed α‑stimulus.
Treat chest pain/ischemia with benzodiazepines (reduce sympathetic surge) and nitrates; consider calcium channel blockers if spasm persists.
Manage seizures with benzodiazepines; avoid phenytoin as it may worsen toxicity.
Aggressive IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis; monitor urine output.
Cool hyperthermia with evaporative methods and antipyretics.
Arrange psychosocial referral for addiction treatment; consider motivational interviewing.

sections.p: After acute care, focus on long‑term harm reduction and monitoring for cardiovascular sequelae.
b: Cardiology review 1–2 weeks after any cardiac event.
Screen for HIV, hepatitis B/C and TB in high‑risk patients.
Counselling on avoiding cocaine and other stimulants.
Referral to community support groups or addiction clinics.
Amphetamine intoxication – similar sympathomimetic signs but longer duration.
Khat (miraa) use – milder stimulant effect, common in East Africa.
Acute coronary syndrome unrelated to drugs – differentiate by toxicology and history.
Normal ECG does not rule out coronary spasm; repeat if symptoms persist.
Negative urine screen may occur if testing is delayed >72 h after use.
Elevated CK can be from seizures or vigorous activity, not only cocaine.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain with ECG changes or troponin rise
Severe hypertension >180/110 mmHg unresponsive to initial therapy
Seizure lasting >5 min or recurrent seizures
Signs of stroke or loss of consciousness

faq.q: Why are β‑blockers avoided in acute cocaine toxicity?
faq.a: β‑blockers block β‑receptors while leaving α‑mediated vasoconstriction unchecked, worsening hypertension and coronary spasm.

faq.q: Can cocaine cause a myocardial infarction in a young person with normal coronaries?
faq.a: Yes, cocaine‑induced coronary vasospasm or thrombosis can precipitate MI even without atherosclerosis.

faq.q: What is the role of benzodiazepines in cocaine overdose?
faq.a: They reduce sympathetic outflow, lower blood pressure, relieve agitation and help control seizures.

exam: A 22‑year‑old presents with sudden chest pain and hypertension after snorting a white powder – what is your immediate management and why avoid pure β‑blockers? — Give benzodiazepine, nitrates, short‑acting calcium channel blocker; explain unopposed α‑stimulation risk.

How would you differentiate cocaine‑induced myocardial infarction from a primary atherosclerotic MI in a low‑resource setting? — Use history of recent use, ECG pattern of transient ST elevation, normal lipid profile; confirm with troponin if available.

A patient develops a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure after cocaine use – what investigations are essential and what do abnormal results indicate? — Check CK (rhabdomyolysis), electrolytes (hyperkalaemia), glucose (hypoglycaemia), and consider repeat ECG for arrhythmia.
Explain why levamisole adulteration is clinically relevant in cocaine users in East Africa. — Levamisole can cause agranulocytosis and vasculitis, presenting with skin necrosis and neutropenia.
What are the key red‑flag signs that mandate transfer to a higher‑level facility? — STEMI, refractory hypertension, status epilepticus, hyperthermia >40 °C, severe rhabdomyolysis with oliguria.

Describe the steps you would take if urine toxicology is unavailable but you strongly suspect cocaine intoxication. — Rely on detailed substance history, characteristic vital signs, ECG changes, and treat empirically with benzodiazepines and antihypertensives.

Why is it important to screen for HIV and hepatitis in a patient presenting with cocaine‑related complications? — High‑risk behaviours increase infection prevalence; co‑infection can affect drug metabolism and organ vulnerability.

Outline a brief counselling plan for a patient who survived a cocaine‑induced stroke. — Discuss trigger avoidance, refer to addiction services, provide education on cardiovascular risk, arrange follow‑up imaging and rehab.
